message.content:
You are working on Nxeon, a VPS/game-server hosting platform, in its live production codebase at /opt/nxeon on this Proxmox host. You have full Bash/Read/Edit/Write access to this real machine. This session just spent a full night finding and fixing real, production-affecting bugs in the multi-node provisioning path (node-2 was just onboarded as a second Proxmox host). The owner now wants a comprehensive, one-by-one integrity sweep of every game in the catalog: provision it for real, verify it's actually reachable, verify a customer can actually change its settings (not just that provisioning "succeeds"), then tear it down completely before moving to the next. This is a genuinely long task (up to ~47 games) — you are running in the background with no time pressure. Be thorough, not fast.

## Why this matters (read this before starting)

Tonight, the first-ever real customer to provision a Minecraft server onto node-2 hit TWO separate, 100%-reproducible bugs that had never been caught because nobody had ever tested a fresh provision against a non-primary node with real rigor:
1. `allocateFreshVmid()` (worker/index.ts) only checked the *target node's own* Proxmox API for taken vmids — blind to orphaned DB rows from other nodes/other cleanups. Fixed by also checking every `Server.vmid` in the DB.
2. The game-port reachability check connected to the guest's *private* IP directly — works on the primary (same bridge network) but the primary has ZERO route to any other node's private subnet (NAT-island architecture). This meant the check was GUARANTEED to fail with EHOSTUNREACH for any non-primary-node game server, forever, regardless of whether the game was actually healthy. Fixed by forwarding the port and checking through the node's own public IP instead.

Separately, that same customer discovered that changing ANY game setting (they needed `online-mode=false` for a non-premium client) fails outright in production: `ENABLE_REAL_GAMECFG` is a global flag that force-enables real settings-application for ALL ~47 game families at once, but `worker/game-config.ts`'s own `REAL_APPLY_FAMILIES` allowlist exists specifically because only `palworld` had ever been individually verified against a real running image — flipping the global flag would activate ~46 untested code paths simultaneously. I (the prior session) just verified `minecraft` the same way palworld was verified: provisioned a real throwaway server, called the apply function directly, read the resulting config file back off disk, confirmed it, then added `"minecraft"` to `REAL_APPLY_FAMILIES` and shipped it.

**Your job is to do this same rigorous verification for the REST of the catalog** — both "does provisioning actually produce a healthy, reachable server" AND "can a customer actually change its settings for real" — one game at a time, fixing what you find, before moving to the next.

Read `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md`'s two newest sections (search for "First real customer provisions onto node-2" and "Migrating a customer VPS/game-server to another node") for the full detail on both bugs above and the general node-2 architecture (NAT-island principle, per-node subnets, etc.) before you start — don't rediscover things already documented.

## Ground truth / exact reference data

- Node-2's id: `cmto2zpwh0000hltqk6oaxy69` (name "node-2", pveNode "nxeon-fsn1", public IP 178.63.94.114). **Every test VM in this sweep goes on node-2, never the primary** — the primary hosts live production traffic and has much less RAM headroom.
- The internal ops account to own every test server: userId `cmrztujaw0002hlazl58i3lsi` (nicholas.sj.albanese@gmail.com) — this is the established convention for internal/test servers on this platform, already used for the free-Minecraft host and tonight's own verification server.
- Full game family list (`lib/games.ts`'s `GAME_FAMILIES`): minecraft, valheim, rust, palworld, cs2, terraria, ark, satisfactory, projectzomboid, sdtd, vrising, enshrouded, factorio, gmod, conan, unturned, theforest, sonsoftheforest, bedrock, schedule1, dragonwilds, sunkenland, abioticfactor, corekeeper, icarus, arkasa, soulmask, dst, vintagestory, necesse, tf2, l4d2, nightingale, squad, spaceengineers, kf2, barotrauma, sandstorm, mordhau, theisle, stationeers, eco, empyrion, plutoniumt4, plutoniumt5, plutoniumt6, plutoniumiw5.
- `minecraft` and `palworld` already have verified, working real-apply config paths (in `REAL_APPLY_FAMILIES` in worker/game-config.ts) — you can skip re-verifying their config-apply, but you SHOULD still do a fresh provisioning+connectivity pass on each (cheap, and confirms nothing regressed).
- `worker/game-config.ts`'s `applyRealConfig()` function has a `switch(family)` with real implementations ALREADY WRITTEN (just never verified+allowlisted) for: `rust`, `valheim`, `cs2` (see `applyRust`, `applyValheim`, `applyCs2` in that file). **These three are your highest-priority targets after minecraft/palworld** — the code exists, it just needs the exact verification minecraft got. Every OTHER family falls to the `default:` case in that switch, meaning **no real-apply code exists at all** for them yet.

## Critical scope boundary — read this carefully

For the ~42 families with NO case in `applyRealConfig`'s switch: **do not write new per-family config-apply implementations from scratch.** Reverse-engineering 42 different games' config file formats, service names, and live-reload mechanisms without any existing pattern to verify against is a separate, much larger engineering project than a verification sweep, and guessing at config paths/formats you can't cross-check against a real spec is exactly how the ORIGINAL unverified code (the one with the `TODO(paths)` comment) came to exist. For these families, your job is: verify provisioning + connectivity are solid (this alone is valuable and exactly mirrors what caught tonight's two real bugs), and clearly note "no real-apply implementation exists for this family (falls to default case in applyRealConfig — settings changes are not possible for this family yet)" as a documented, known gap. That is a legitimate, useful finding — not a failure on your part to fix everything.

## Per-game procedure

For each family, in this order — do `minecraft`, `palworld` first (quick regression check only), then `rust`, `valheim`, `cs2` (full config-apply verification, matching minecraft's treatment), then work through the remaining ~42 alphabetically or in the order listed above (provisioning + connectivity only, plus the "no real-apply" note):

### 1. Provision a real throwaway server

```js
const db = require("./lib/db").db; // or `import` in a .ts script run via `npx tsx`
const node2Id = "cmto2zpwh0000hltqk6oaxy69";
const gamePlan = await db.gamePlan.findFirst({ where: { gameFamily: "<family>" }, orderBy: { priceCents: "asc" } });
if (!gamePlan) { /* record "no gamePlan exists for this family — skip", move on */ }
const server = await db.server.create({ data: {
  name: `test-${family}-${Date.now()}`, hostname: `test-${family}-${Date.now()}`.slice(0, 40),
  userId: "cmrztujaw0002hlazl58i3lsi",
  planId: gamePlan.basePlanId, osTemplateId: gamePlan.osTemplateId, gamePlanId: gamePlan.id,
  nodeId: node2Id, isFree: true, termPromoPercent: 100,
}});
await db.job.create({ data: { type: "PROVISION", serverId: server.id } });
```
Hostname must match `/^[a-z0-9]([a-z0-9-]*[a-z0-9])?$/i` and be ≤40 chars — sanitize the family name + timestamp accordingly (e.g. strip nothing, family names here are already lowercase alnum).

### 2. Wait for the job (poll, don't sleep-chain)

Poll `db.job.findFirst({ where: { serverId, type: "PROVISION" }, orderBy: { createdAt: "desc" } })` every ~5s via a `run_in_background` bash loop (an `until` loop that exits when status is DONE or FAILED), not manual chained sleeps. Minecraft/Palworld-class games provision in 1-3 minutes; some larger game images may take longer (5-10+ min) — be patient, this is a background task.

If the job FAILS: this is exactly the kind of bug tonight found twice. Read the error, SSH into the guest (get connection details via `db.server.findUnique({ where: { id }, select: { rootPassword: true, rootPasswordEnc: true, sshPort: true, dedicatedIp: { select: { address: true } }, node: { select: { publicIp: true } } } })`, decrypt via `lib/crypto-box.ts`'s `decryptSecret()`, then `sshpass -f <local-file-never-inline> ssh -p <sshPort> root@<node.publicIp>`), find the actual root cause the same way tonight's session did (check `docker ps`, `journalctl`, actual listening ports via `ss -tlnp`/`ss -ulnp`), and if it's a real, general bug (not specific to this one game's image being broken) — fix it in the shared code following the FULL discipline below. If it turns out to be something specific to that one game's Docker image/template being broken (not a platform bug), just document it clearly and move on — you are not responsible for fixing third-party game server images.

### 3. Verify real connectivity (not just "job said DONE")

- SSH: `sshpass` connect to `<node.publicIp>:<sshPort>` as root, confirm it responds.
- Game port: read `lib/games.ts`'s `GAME_PORT` map for this family's `{port, protocol}` — this is the SAME map the provisioning health check itself uses, so testing against it validates the exact same contract. Check `db.portForward.findMany({ where: { serverId, guestPort: GAME_PORT[family].port } })` for the allocated public port, then do a real external test from this box (raw TCP connect via `nc -zv` for tcp, or a raw UDP packet send + tcpdump-inside-guest capture for udp, exactly like tonight's session did for Palworld/Rust — see the "Prove reachability for real" section of the migration doc referenced above).
- Also SSH in and directly confirm the actual game process/container is running (`docker ps`, or `systemctl status <unit>` per `worker/game-control.ts`'s `controlSpec`/`serviceHints` for that family) and check its own logs for a clean startup (no crash loop, no obvious fatal errors) — don't just trust the port being open.

### 4. Verify settings changes actually work (the NEW, critical part)

Check `worker/game-config.ts`'s `applyRealConfig` switch for a case matching this family.

**If a case exists** (rust, valheim, cs2 — plus minecraft/palworld already done): temporarily add `export` to `applyRealConfig` if not already exported (it already is, from tonight's minecraft work — check first), write a small script that imports it directly and calls it with 1-2 real settings from `lib/game-config.ts`'s `schemaFor(family).fields` (pick fields that exist in that family's schema — read the schema first, don't guess field names), then **read the actual resulting config file back off disk via SSH** to confirm the values genuinely changed — exactly the standard tonight's minecraft verification used. If this works cleanly, add the family to `REAL_APPLY_FAMILIES` in worker/game-config.ts (with a comment documenting what you verified and how, matching the existing palworld/minecraft comments' style) and ship it (see deploy discipline below). If you find a real bug in the existing `applyRust`/`applyValheim`/`applyCs2` code (e.g., wrong config path, wrong format, a bug like palworld's "regenerate-then-lose writes" from yesterday), fix it the same way, re-verify, then allowlist it.

**If no case exists** (the other ~42): do not implement one. Just record the finding.

### 5. Full teardown — every time, success or failure

```bash
qm stop <vmid>   # on node-2 via: ssh root@178.63.94.114 'qm stop <vmid>; sleep 3; qm destroy <vmid> --purge 1 --destroy-unreferenced-disks 1'
```
This is a destructive action and the permission classifier may ask you to confirm it (via AskUserQuestion) since it's a VM destroy — that's expected and fine, answer that it's your own throwaway test VM with zero customer impact, matching exactly what tonight's session did. If a destroy gets blocked and you can't get confirmation (background execution may not always surface an interactive prompt), note it clearly in your final report as "test VM <vmid> for <family> needs manual cleanup" and move on — do not let one blocked cleanup stall the whole sweep.

Then delete the DB rows completely — **this is the single most important lesson from tonight, learn it well**: a `qm destroy` that doesn't ALSO delete the `Server` row (and its `Job`/`PortForward` rows) leaves an orphaned row holding a vmid that will collide with a real future customer's provision, exactly as happened twice tonight (`ggjgjhgjghh`, `movieshack` — both from a THREE-WEEK-OLD disk-only cleanup that never touched the DB). Do this for every single test server, no exceptions:
```js
await db.portForward.deleteMany({ where: { serverId } });
await db.job.deleteMany({ where: { serverId } });
await db.server.delete({ where: { id: serverId } });
```

## Deploy discipline for any real code fix

Never skip steps. For every fix: `npx tsc --noEmit -p .` (must be clean) → `npx tsx --test test/*.test.ts` (baseline is 1318 pass / 34 fail — that 34 is pre-existing and unrelated to anything in this codebase area; investigate anything ELSE that fails) → `git add <specific files>` (never `-A`, there are unrelated uncommitted files from other work in this tree — check `git status` and only stage what you touched) → commit with a clear message explaining the bug and the fix → `bash scripts/deploy-staging.sh` → confirm HTTP 200 → `bash scripts/promote-production.sh` → confirm HTTP 200. Both deploy scripts run for a few minutes; run them with a background bash task and wait for completion rather than assuming success.

## Safety rails (non-negotiable)

- Node-2 only, for every test VM. Never the primary.
- Only ever touch Server rows you created yourself in this sweep. Never modify, restart, or inspect any real customer's server.
- Never print/inline a password or token into a visible command string — write secrets to a local scratch file first (e.g. under a scratchpad dir) and reference the file, exactly like every SSH auth in this session tonight.
- If you hit something that seems to need a business/product decision rather than a pure technical fix (e.g., "should we support this game at all", pricing, anything ambiguous), don't guess — write it clearly into your final report as needing the owner's decision, and move on to the next game rather than blocking the whole sweep.
- If overall host capacity on node-2 ever looks tight (`free -h` via `ssh root@178.63.94.114`), pause and check `qm list` for anything you forgot to tear down before continuing — don't let leaked test VMs accumulate.

## Reporting

Keep a running progress log (a plain markdown or JSON file under this session's scratch area is fine) as you go, so partial progress is legible even if you're interrupted — one entry per family: status (verified-full / verified-provisioning-only / no-gameplan-exists / failed-needs-owner-decision), what was tested, what was found, what was fixed (with commit hashes) if anything.

For every REAL bug you find and fix, add a short section to `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` immediately (matching this session's own established practice — search the file for "## " headers to see the style/tone of existing entries), not batched at the end. Commit doc-only changes as their own commit, same as tonight's session did.

At the end, produce a clear final summary: how many families fully verified (provisioning + connectivity + config-apply), how many verified provisioning+connectivity only (with the "no real-apply exists" note), any real bugs found and fixed (with what changed), any families skipped and why (no gamePlan, needs owner decision, etc.), and the final state of `REAL_APPLY_FAMILIES`.

- figma:figma-code-connect: Creates and maintains Figma Code Connect template files that map Figma components to code snippets. Use when the user mentions Code Connect, Figma component mapping, design-to-code translation, or asks to create/update .figma.ts or .figma.js files.
- figma:figma-create-new-file: **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE every `create_new_file` tool call. NEVER call `create_new_file` directly without loading this skill first. Trigger whenever the user wants a new blank Figma file — a new design, FigJam, or Slides file — or when you need a fresh file before calling `use_figma`. Usage — /figma-create-new-file [editorType] [fileName] (e.g. /figma-create-new-file figjam My Whiteboard, /figma-create-new-file slides Q3 Review)
- figma:figma-design-to-code: **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE calling the `get_design_context` Figma MCP tool. You MUST trigger this skill whenever the user wants to implement, build, port, or code up a Figma design as code. Example prompts (not exhaustive) are 'implement this Figma design', 'build this screen from Figma', 'turn this Figma into code', 'design to code'. This skill provides critical instructions and steps to the agent on how to correctly implement Figma designs in code and must NOT be skipped.
- figma:figma-generate-design: Use this skill alongside figma-use when the task involves translating an application page, view, or multi-section layout into Figma. Triggers: 'write to Figma', 'create in Figma from code', 'push page to Figma', 'take this app/page and build it in Figma', 'create a screen', 'build a landing page in Figma', 'update the Figma screen to match code', 'convert this modal/dialog/drawer/panel to Figma'. This is the preferred workflow skill whenever the user wants to build or update a full page, modal, dialog, drawer, sidebar, panel, or any composed multi-section view in Figma from code or a description. Discovers design system components, variables, and styles from Code Connect files, existing screens, and library search, then imports them and assembles views incrementally section-by-section using design system tokens instead of hardcoded values.
- figma:figma-generate-diagram: MANDATORY prerequisite — load this skill BEFORE every `generate_diagram` tool call. NEVER call `generate_diagram` directly without loading this skill first. Trigger whenever the user asks to create, generate, draw, render, sketch, or build a diagram — flowchart, architecture diagram, sequence diagram, ERD or entity-relationship diagram, state diagram or state machine, gantt chart, or timeline. Also trigger when the user mentions Mermaid syntax or wants a system architecture, decision tree, dependency graph, API call flow, auth handshake, schema, or pipeline visualized in FigJam. Routes to type-specific guidance, sets universal Mermaid constraints, and tells you when to use a different diagram type or skip the tool entirely (mindmaps, pie charts, class diagrams, etc.).
- figma:figma-generate-library: Build or update a professional-grade design system in Figma from a codebase. Use when the user wants to create variables/tokens, build component libraries, create individual components with proper variant sets and variable bindings, set up theming (light/dark modes), document foundations, or reconcile gaps between code and Figma. Also use when the user asks to create or generate any component in Figma — even a single one — since components require proper variable foundations, variant states, and design token bindings to be production-quality. This skill teaches WHAT to build and in WHAT ORDER — it complements the `figma-use` skill which teaches HOW to call the Plugin API. Both skills should be loaded together.
- figma:figma-implement-motion: Translates Figma motion and animations into production-ready application code. ## Migrating a customer VPS/game-server to another node (2026-09-06)

Primary hit CRITICAL RAM again (see [[nxeon-node-ram-tuning]] for the full incident — a
real, host-level OOM-kill of a customer VM's own kvm process, twice in one day). Fixed by
migrating three non-dedicated-IP servers to node-2: **sausaugepro** (Palworld, 117→101),
**rust-w75hko** (Rust, 113→102), and **kaymofilms-vps** (plain VPS + website, 116→103,
resized 4096→2048MB RAM first). All three completed with zero customer-visible downtime.
This section is the general runbook — the free-MC migration (see the section above) was
the first proof this worked at all; this one is what surfaced the sharp edges that only
show up on servers with a real, individual customer footprint.

### The runbook

1. **vzdump** on the source node, `--mode snapshot --compress zstd`, into a real disk path
   with room (`/var/lib/vz/<something>` — **never `/root`**, which is a small `md3` root
   partition; a single 80GB VM's backup exhausted its 14GB free space mid-write and aborted
   the job, though the live VM resumed cleanly with no damage). `df -h` the target before
   starting a multi-VM batch.
2. **scp the archive to the target node.** Cross-region transfers (this primary is OVH
   Singapore, node-2 is Hetzner Falkenstein) are slow — budget minutes per 10-15GB, not
   seconds. Target a real disk path on the destination too, not `/tmp` if it's tmpfs
   (it was here — 32GB RAM-backed — fine for one file, risky as a habit for larger/parallel
   transfers).
3. **Move the archive into the destination storage's `dump/` subdirectory** (e.g.
   `/mnt/pve/vmdata-hdd/dump/`), not the storage root — `qmrestore` looks for backups in the
   storage's tracked content path specifically.
4. **`qmrestore <archive> <new-vmid> --storage <images-storage>`** (e.g. `vmdata`, not the
   backup-content storage). Get the new vmid from `pvesh get /cluster/nextid`, but see the
   vmid-collision gotcha below before trusting it blindly.
5. **Fix networking on the restored config, before starting it**: `qm set <vmid> --delete
   cicustom` (the snippet path is a primary-only pmxcfs reference — see Phase 1's writeup
   above; safe to delete because the disk is already fully realized, unlike a fresh
   template clone) and `qm set <vmid> --ipconfig0 ip=<new-node-subnet>/24,gw=<new-gw>`.
6. **Start it, confirm the new IP via `qm guest cmd <vmid> network-get-interfaces`** — don't
   trust the config file alone; confirm cloud-init actually re-applied it inside the guest.
7. **Update the DB**: `Server.nodeId`, `Server.vmid`, `Server.ipAddress`. Do this *before*
   allocating any new port forwards for the server (the allocator and the NAT sync both key
   off the current `nodeId`).
8. **Run `syncPortForwards()`** (`worker/network.ts`) once, manually, rather than waiting
   for the next worker cycle — it reconciles every node independently, so this is safe to
   call directly. It will show the old node's stale rules being deleted and the new node's
   rules being added; read the numbers, don't just assume success.
9. **Prove reachability for real, per port, don't just trust the rule existing**: for TCP
   (SSH), an actual `ssh -p <port> root@<new-public-ip>` from a genuinely different host.
   For UDP game ports (no real handshake to piggyback on), send a raw UDP packet from
   outside and confirm BOTH the NAT rule's packet counter incremented (`iptables -t nat -L
   ... -n -v`) AND a `tcpdump` inside the guest, on the exact port, shows "received by
   filter: N" ≥ 1 — the DNAT counter alone only proves the *host* matched the rule, not
   that the packet actually reached the guest.
10. **Only stop the old VM once the new one is independently verified working** — vzdump
    snapshot mode never stops the source, so both copies are live simultaneously during the
    whole verification window. This is what makes zero-downtime possible: the cutover
    moment is "when you update the config that routes to it" (DNS/nginx/NAT), not "when you
    start the new VM" — the two can be minutes apart with no gap in service.

### Three real, non-obvious things this audit found (the reason a "full audit" beat a
### "trust the standard steps" migration)

1. **A pre-existing, unrelated bug**: rust-w75hko's Rust container was fully healthy and
   listening correctly on both its ports (28015/udp join, 28016/tcp RCON) — confirmed via
   `ss` inside the guest — but had **zero NAT forward for either port**, on the DB or the
   live iptables, on the primary, before this migration ever started. `lib/ipam.ts`'s
   `allocateGameForward()` exists specifically to prevent this class of bug (its own doc
   comment describes finding the identical issue on a Minecraft server previously), but
   this Rust server evidently never got it called for it — a real, live, paying customer
   had zero player connectivity for who knows how long. Fixed by calling
   `allocateGameForward()` for the missing port as part of setting up node-2's config —
   migrating it *fixed* the customer's pre-existing outage as a side effect, rather than
   faithfully reproducing a broken state.
2. **A cross-node dependency invisible to every check except reading the actual configs**:
   kaymofilms-vps has a live customer website (kaymofilms.com). TLS termination and the
   public-facing vhost run on the **primary's own nginx** (`/etc/nginx/sites-available/
   kaymofilms`), which reverse-proxies to the guest's private IP: `proxy_pass
   http://10.20.0.103:80`. This is a completely separate mechanism from the
   PortForward/NAT system (SSH and game ports all checked out perfectly fine) — DNS points
   at the *primary's* public IP, not the guest's, and the guest is only ever reached
   internally, over the private bridge. Migrating the VM without touching this file would
   have broken the website the instant the old VM stopped, with every other check (SSH,
   internal nginx health, even a direct curl to the guest's own IP) still looking
   completely healthy. The NAT-island principle means primary literally cannot route to
   node-2's private subnet at all — the fix is to allocate a `PortForward` for port 80 on
   the *new* node (same as any other port) and repoint `proxy_pass` at the new node's
   *public* IP and forwarded port, not its private IP. **Any customer-domain website
   hosted on a NAT (non-dedicated-IP) server needs its host nginx vhost checked for a
   hardcoded backend IP before that VM is ever moved to a different node** — grep
   `/etc/nginx/sites-available/` for the server's current private IP as a standing step in
   this runbook, not an afterthought.
3. **A cross-node vmid collision from a two-week-old orphaned DB row**: assigning the
   restored Rust VM's real Proxmox vmid (102, node-2) to the DB hit a unique-constraint
   error — an unrelated, already-`SUSPENDED`, gibberish-named test row
   (`ggjgjhgjghh`) already held `vmid: 102` in the database, even though the *actual*
   Proxmox VM 102 on the primary had been destroyed weeks earlier (2026-08-21's RAM
   cleanup, per [[nxeon-node-ram-tuning]]) — its disk was purged but its `Server` row
   never deleted. This is exactly the "`nodeId: null` vmid-collision risk" the original
   multi-node audit plan flagged as a known hazard, just manifesting via a stale `vmid`
   instead. Fixed by nulling the orphan's `vmid` (with the owner's sign-off — this is a
   direct prod DB mutation) rather than picking an arbitrary different vmid, which would
   have left the DB's vmid permanently out of sync with the real Proxmox identity.
   **Standing lesson: any future orphan-VM cleanup must delete the DB `Server` row, not just
   `qm destroy` the Proxmox VM** — a disk-only cleanup leaves a landmine for the next vmid
   reuse, on any node, indefinitely.

### One more real gotcha: password mismatch after snapshot restore

rust-w75hko's restored copy rejected its known-correct root password (`pam_unix:
authentication failure`, confirmed genuine via verbose SSH logs and by re-verifying the
same password worked against the still-live original seconds later) — sausaugepro and
kaymofilms-vps's restores did NOT show this, so it isn't universal. Root cause undetermined
(the disk is a live snapshot of the identical filesystem, so a byte-for-byte password-hash
difference is surprising). **Fix used**: reset the password via the hypervisor's
guest-agent channel — `qm guest passwd <vmid> root` (reads the new password from stdin as
two newline-terminated lines, not a CLI argument — `printf '%s\n%s\n' "$pw" "$pw" | qm
guest passwd ...`) — which works without needing any existing credential, then update
`Server.rootPasswordEnc` to match. This is the correct recovery technique generally: verify
SSH access to a freshly-restored guest as an explicit step, don't assume a snapshot
guarantees credential parity. **This mutates a live credential, so it needs owner sign-off
per [[nxeon-live-credential-rotation-policy]]** even though it's a clean, well-understood
fix — which is exactly what happened here.

## Embedded Checkout's 3D Secure iframe: a fallback to hosted Checkout on genuine embed failure (2026-09-05)

Investigating a customer (`sorenshabnam93@gmail.com`) whose $32.99 order payment failed: Stripe's
dashboard showed `3D Secure attempt failed` only **15 seconds** after the customer was asked to
authenticate — too fast for a real completed (or even attempted) bank challenge. Root cause:
checkout runs Stripe's **embedded** Checkout (`ui_mode: "embedded_page"`,
`CheckoutElementsProvider`/`PaymentElement` per `components/customer/PaymentStep.tsx`), which mounts
card entry AND the 3DS challenge inside an iframe on our own page — not a full-page redirect to
Stripe/the bank. That architecture is the right default (no jarring redirect, matches the rest of the
wizard), but it's measurably less robust than a full-page redirect for a real slice of traffic:
ad-blockers/privacy extensions that specifically target embedded payment iframes, Safari's
cross-site-cookie restrictions, and mobile in-app browsers (a link opened from
Instagram/TikTok/Facebook) all have documented trouble rendering a **nested** 3DS challenge. The
15-second timing is consistent with the iframe never successfully loading, not the customer
attempting and failing a real challenge.

A broader look at recent Stripe cancellations found this is NOT the majority pattern — most
"cancelled" checkouts (checked several from `wizzy.zelda@gmail.com`, `ddm43090@gmail.com`) never had
a payment method attached at all; they're ordinary window-shopping abandonment that Stripe
auto-expires ~1h later, already covered by the generic `deploy_winback` re-engagement email. Only a
small subset actually attempt to pay and hit friction — that subset is the one this fix targets, and
the one the existing `checkout.session.expired`/`checkout.session.completed`-only webhook
(`app/api/stripe/webhook/route.ts`) has zero visibility into (no `payment_intent.payment_failed`
handling exists — a real, separate gap, not yet built, flagged for later).

**Fix:** `createHostedFallbackFromSession()` (`lib/stripe.ts`) rebuilds a still-open embedded session
as a classic hosted one — same customer, same line items, same metadata (so the existing
`fulfilCheckoutSession` dispatch handles it completely unchanged regardless of order type; this
required zero changes to any of the six-plus `createXCheckout` functions). Exposed via
`getHostedCheckoutFallback()` (`lib/actions-payment-fallback.ts`), which checks the session's
`metadata.nxeonUserId` against the calling user before handing back a link — the same ownership field
every order type already stamps.

**Deliberately narrow, per explicit owner instruction — offered ONLY when the embed itself appears to
have broken, never proactively and never on an ordinary decline.** `PaymentStep.tsx`'s `payWithCard()`
already had two distinct outcomes from `checkoutActions.confirm()`: a clean `result.type === "error"`
(a real decline — insufficient funds, wrong CVC, etc., where "try another card" is already the correct
message) versus the `catch` block (an unexpected thrown exception — the signal that `confirm()` itself
broke rather than the bank saying no). The fallback link is fetched and shown ONLY in that `catch`
branch.

Verified against a real, currently-open live checkout session by reconstructing it end-to-end and
reading the new session back: correct `ui_mode: "hosted_page"`, same customer, same metadata, same
line item/amount, correct `success_url`. Both the real session used for the read-only check and the
synthetic order-shaped test session created to verify the "has line items" path were left/expired
untouched — no live customer checkout was disturbed.

## Failed-payment recovery: `payment_intent.payment_failed` webhook + a targeted retry email (2026-09-05)

Direct follow-up to the embedded-Checkout 3DS fallback above. Before this, `app/api/stripe/webhook`
handled exactly two event types (`checkout.session.completed`, `checkout.session.expired`) — a real
payment FAILURE was invisible to us entirely; the only reason `sorenshabnam93`'s case was ever found
was a human manually opening the Stripe dashboard.

**Deliberately narrow, matching the fallback link's own scope:** most Stripe cancellations are
ordinary declines (wrong CVC, insufficient funds) that Stripe's own checkout UI already shows inline
in the moment — those get no follow-up here, by design. The new handler
(`lib/payment-failed-recovery.ts`'s `handleFailedPaymentIntent`) filters to exactly one Stripe error
code: `last_payment_error.code === "payment_intent_authentication_failure"` — the specific,
Stripe-documented signal that the 3D Secure/bank-authentication step stalled. That's the same failure
class the hosted-fallback fix targets, just caught server-side after the fact instead of client-side
in the moment.

**Flow:** find the Checkout Session behind the failed PaymentIntent (`stripe.checkout.sessions.list({
payment_intent })`) — this is where `nxeonUserId` and every other Nxeon field already lives, so
(same as the hosted fallback) zero changes were needed to any of the six-plus `createXCheckout`
functions. Look up the user, send `emails.checkoutPaymentRetry` — a NEW template, distinct from the
existing `paymentFailed` (which is about an EXISTING customer's recurring/renewal charge failing, with
a "update your payment method" CTA — wrong shape for "a new order never finished," which needs a link
to finish THAT SPECIFIC order instead). If the original session is still `open`, the email's link is a
freshly-generated `createHostedFallbackFromSession` hosted-Checkout URL; otherwise it points at the
generic deploy page.

**Kind:** sent as `payment_action_required` — already a CRITICAL, non-suppressible `NotifyKind` in
`lib/prefs.ts` ("3-D Secure / `requires_action` — the payment stalls until the customer acts"),
existing before this fix but previously unused for this purpose. Correct: this is the customer's own
in-flight purchase, not marketing.

**Dedupe:** the EmailLog `template` field is free-form once `html` is supplied directly (confirmed by
reading `sendMail`'s own dispatch — it only renders from `template` when `html` is absent), so
`checkout_payment_retry:${paymentIntentId}` doubles as a per-attempt idempotency key against Stripe
webhook redelivery, with zero schema change.

content.content:
## First real customer provisions onto node-2 surfaced two more bugs (2026-09-06)

A real Minecraft order (node-2, no dedicated IP — the same eligibility class as the RAM-relief
migrations above) failed provisioning 3 times running into two separate, previously-latent bugs.
Both are architectural, not node-2-specific quirks — fixed once in the shared provisioning code,
so they can't recur on this or any future node.

1. **`allocateFreshVmid()` only checked the target node's own Proxmox API for taken vmids.** Each
   node is a separate, non-clustered Proxmox install, so it has zero visibility into vmids used on
   *other* nodes, and zero visibility into a DB row whose Proxmox VM was `qm destroy`'d without the
   row being cleaned up. `Server.vmid` is unique across the whole app, not per node — that's the
   actual source of truth to check. Hit live twice in a row (node-2 offering 102, then 104, each
   already held by an orphaned row from the 2026-08-21 RAM cleanup — see
   [[nxeon-node-ram-tuning]]). Fixed by also pulling every `Server.vmid` from the DB into the
   allocator's "taken" set. Cleared both orphaned rows (`ggjgjhgjghh`, `movieshack`) in the process.
   **Standing lesson: any future orphan-VM cleanup must delete the DB row, not just `qm destroy` the
   VM**, or the next vmid reuse — on any node — hits the same wall.

2. **The provisioning game-port reachability check connected to the guest's PRIVATE ip directly.**
   Correct on the primary (the worker shares its own bridge network), but the primary has NO route
   to any other node's private subnet at all (the NAT-island principle — see the multi-node section
   above). This made the check fail with `EHOSTUNREACH` on literally 100% of attempts for a
   non-primary node, regardless of whether the game server was actually healthy — confirmed live:
   SSH already correctly checks the public address and passed every time, while the game-port check
   failed every time even though the customer's Minecraft server was demonstrably running and
   listening the whole time (confirmed via direct SSH). Fixed by forwarding the game port BEFORE
   checking (reusing an existing forward on retry, not leaking a new public port every attempt) and
   checking through the node's own public IP — the same external path the SSH check already proved
   works. Primary behavior is untouched.

### A third, unrelated finding on the same order: `ENABLE_REAL_GAMECFG` was globally off

The customer needed `online-mode=false` (a non-premium/TLauncher client) and used the dashboard's
settings toggle — which failed outright with "real application is switched off on this server
(ENABLE_REAL_GAMECFG is not set)... Please contact support." Fixed the one server by hand
(`server.properties` + a restart) to unblock them immediately, then looked into the flag itself.

**`ENABLE_REAL_GAMECFG=1` is a blanket switch — it force-enables EVERY game family's real-apply path
at once.** `worker/game-config.ts`'s own `REAL_APPLY_FAMILIES` allowlist exists precisely so a
family only goes live once its actual apply logic has been confirmed against the real running image
— not just read for correctness — and only `palworld` had ever cleared that bar (2026-09-05, after
a real bug was found in an earlier version: it silently regenerated its own config from env vars on
every boot, losing writes it had just made). Flipping the global flag would have activated ~46 other
untested families' real-apply code simultaneously — exactly the "reports success, nothing actually
happened" failure class this whole night has been about.

Verified `minecraft` the same way: provisioned a real throwaway server on node-2, called
`applyRealConfig` directly with `difficulty` + `online-mode`, then read
`/opt/mc/server.properties` back off disk and confirmed both values — then destroyed the VM and
deleted its DB row (no orphan left behind, learning directly from finding #1 above). The
`applyMinecraft` code's own `TODO(paths)` comment turned out to be resolved for the current image:
the host-side bind mount (`/opt/mc` → `/data`) puts `server.properties` somewhere the locate logic's
`find` over `/opt` already reaches. One real, non-blocking gap found along the way: `mcrcon` isn't
installed on the Minecraft image, so live (no-restart) RCON pushes for fields like `difficulty`
always fall back to "restart to apply" — correctly reported as such, never silently claimed live.
Added `minecraft` to `REAL_APPLY_FAMILIES`. **The global flag is still off** — every other family
remains unverified and should get the same live, read-it-back-off-disk treatment before being added
individually, rather than flipping the blanket switch.

---

(server migration).*

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Poll a PROVISION job until it reaches DONE or FAILED (or the deadline).
# Usage: wait.sh <serverId> [maxSeconds]
set -u
SW=/tmp/claude-0/-root/4f329df3-66ee-49c8-a6c5-615ecf189efc/scratchpad/sweep
SID="$1"
MAX="${2:-1800}"
cd /opt/nxeon
START=$(date +%s)
LAST=""
until false; do
  OUT=$(npx tsx "$SW/status.ts" "$SID" 2>&1)
  ST=$(printf '%s' "$OUT" | python3 -c 'import sys,json;d=json.load(sys.stdin);print((d.get("job") or {}).get("status",""))' 2>/dev/null)
  STEP=$(printf '%s' "$OUT" | python3 -c 'import sys,json;d=json.load(sys.stdin);print((d.get("server") or {}).get("provisioningStep") or "")' 2>/dev/null)
  NOW=$(date +%s); EL=$((NOW-START))
  if [ "$ST$STEP" != "$LAST" ]; then
    echo "[${EL}s] job=$ST step=$STEP"
    LAST="$ST$STEP"
  fi
  case "$ST" in
    DONE|FAILED) echo "FINAL after ${EL}s:"; printf '%s\n' "$OUT"; exit 0 ;;
  esac
  if [ "$EL" -ge "$MAX" ]; then echo "TIMEOUT after ${EL}s:"; printf '%s\n' "$OUT"; exit 2; fi
  sleep 5
done

For the longer polling waits, I'll rely on run_in_background so I get notified on completion, which matches the intended pattern for monitoring these multi-minute checks.

Given roughly 42 games each taking several minutes, this sweep will realistically take hours, which lines up with expectations for this kind of long-running verification task. To be more efficient I'm considering pipelining — starting provisioning for the next game while still verifying the current one — though the instructions call for genuine per-game reachability verification, not shortcuts.

I decide the safest approach is strictly one game at a time using a foreground wait script with a bounded timeout, re-running it if it times out, rather than juggling background monitoring — simpler to reason about and avoids resource contention.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Prove a UDP game port is reachable END TO END: send raw UDP from THIS box to the
# node's public IP:publicPort and confirm (a) the node's DNAT rule counter moved and
# (b) tcpdump INSIDE the guest saw the packets on the guest port.
# Usage: udpcheck.sh <serverId> <sshHost=nodePublicIp> <sshPort> <publicPort> <guestPort>
set -u
SW=/tmp/claude-0/-root/4f329df3-66ee-49c8-a6c5-615ecf189efc/scratchpad/sweep
SID="$1"; HOST="$2"; SPORT="$3"; PUBPORT="$4"; GPORT="$5"
CAP="$SW/cap-$SID.txt"

# NAT counter before
echo "=== node DNAT rule (before) ==="
ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o ConnectTimeout=15 "root@$HOST" \
  "iptables -t nat -L NXEON_FWD_N2 -n -v --line-numbers 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'dpt:$PUBPORT( |\$)' || echo '(no rule found for dpt:$PUBPORT)'"

# tcpdump inside the guest, in the background locally
( bash "$SW/connect.sh" "$SID" "$HOST" "$SPORT" \
    "command -v tcpdump >/dev/null 2>&1 || (apt-get install -y -qq tcpdump >/dev/null 2>&1); timeout 20 tcpdump -ni any -c 4 udp port $GPORT 2>&1" \
    > "$CAP" 2>&1 ) &
CAPPID=$!

sleep 6
echo "=== sending UDP probes to $HOST:$PUBPORT ==="
for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do
  printf 'nxeon-reachability-probe' | timeout 2 nc -u -w1 "$HOST" "$PUBPORT" >/dev/null 2>&1
  sleep 1
done

wait $CAPPID 2>/dev/null
echo "=== tcpdump inside the guest (port $GPORT) ==="
cat "$CAP"

echo "=== node DNAT rule (after) ==="
ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o ConnectTimeout=15 "root@$HOST" \
  "iptables -t nat -L NXEON_FWD_N2 -n -v --line-numbers 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'dpt:$PUBPORT( |\$)' || echo '(no rule found for dpt:$PUBPORT)'"

I'm confirming that `wrapDockerGameService` converts every game family's `docker run -d` into a `docker create` plus a systemd unit with `Restart=always`, meaning systemd, not docker's own restart policy, is the platform's real supervision mechanism—so it deliberately strips `--restart`. And even when things go right, the freshly recreated container is created outside systemd via `docker run -d`, leaving `palworld.service` stuck in a failed or inactive state, which would break the control panel's power buttons since those rely on `systemctl start/stop/restart`.

## Game-config apply fought systemd for control of the container (2026-09-06)

Found during the whole-catalog integrity sweep, on the very first family checked after Minecraft:
`applyPalworld` (`worker/game-config.ts`) manipulated the game container **through docker
directly**, but docker is not what supervises it.

**Every game family's container is owned by systemd, not docker.** `worker/index.ts`'s
`wrapDockerGameService()` rewrites each family's `docker run -d --name X ...` setup script at
PROVISION time into `docker create` plus a `<hint>.service` unit
(`ExecStart=/usr/bin/docker start -a X`, `Restart=always`, `RestartSec=5`), and it deliberately
**strips docker's own `--restart` policy** — in its own words, because "leaving both in place makes
the two supervisors fight over a crash-looping process". That wrapper applies to all 47 families, so
this is the platform-wide lifecycle model, not a Palworld quirk.

Two concrete defects followed from talking to the wrong supervisor, both confirmed live against a
real throwaway Palworld server on node-2 (not reasoned about — provisioned, applied, journal read):

1. **The revival race the previous fix claimed to have closed was still half-open.** The
   2026-09-05 fix disabled docker's `unless-stopped` policy before stopping the container, and its
   comment says that "closes the race entirely". It closes docker's half. systemd's half was
   untouched: `docker stop palworld` makes the unit's `ExecStart` (`docker start -a palworld`) exit,
   systemd calls that an unexpected failure, and `Restart=always`/`RestartSec=5` re-runs it five
   seconds later. Straight out of the guest's own journal during an apply:
   `05:23:19 palworld.service: Deactivated successfully.` →
   `05:23:24 palworld.service: Scheduled restart job, restart counter is at 1.`
   So the function had a **5-second budget** to finish its `rename` + recreate before systemd
   revived the container it was in the middle of replacing. It won every race I ran, but nothing
   made it win; a slow `docker create` (busy host, cold cache) loses, and losing lands in the
   rollback path — a customer's settings change failing for no reason they could ever see.
2. **Every successful apply permanently double-supervised the container.** The recreate used
   `docker run -d ... --restart unless-stopped`, re-adding exactly the policy
   `wrapDockerGameService` strips. Confirmed on the real container after an apply:
   `restart=unless-stopped`, alongside a still-`enabled` `palworld.service`. From that moment on
   that customer's server had two supervisors for the rest of its life — the precise state the
   provisioning code exists to prevent. (Reboot and `docker kill` tests both happened to converge,
   with systemd winning; the damage here is latent, not yet customer-visible, which is why nothing
   had ever reported it.)

**Fix:** a shared `resolveGameUnit(conn, family)` helper resolves the supervising unit from
`lib/game-control.ts`'s per-family `controlSpec().serviceHints` — the same list
`wrapDockerGameService` names the unit from and `worker/game-control.ts`'s power buttons resolve
against, so it cannot drift from the unit that actually got installed. `applyPalworld` now drives
the lifecycle through it: `systemctl stop` (which runs the unit's own `ExecStop` **and** marks the
unit explicitly stopped, so `Restart=always` genuinely does not fire — this is the only thing that
closes the race, rather than racing it), then `docker create` with **no** `--restart` flag, then
`systemctl start`. It also now confirms the container is actually `.State.Running` before deleting
the old one — `systemctl start` returns as soon as it forks `docker start -a`, so a zero exit proved
only that the unit launched, and a container that died immediately afterwards would have had its
rollback target already deleted.

`resolveGameUnit` returning null (a server provisioned before that wrapper shipped, or a setup
script that never matched its shape) keeps the old direct-docker path verbatim, `--restart
unless-stopped` included — there docker's policy really is the only supervisor and must be
preserved.

**Verified live, before and after**, on a real node-2 Palworld server: four settings written and
read back off `/opt/palworld/Pal/Saved/Config/LinuxServer/PalWorldSettings.ini`
(`Difficulty=Difficult`, `ExpRate=4.000000`, `bIsPvP=False`, `ServerPlayerMaxNum=11`), container
`restart=no`, unit `active` with `NRestarts: 0` and `Result: success`, no stray `palworld-old`
container, and a journal showing a clean intentional `Stopping → Stopped → Started` instead of the
old `Deactivated → Scheduled restart job → restart counter is at 1`.

**Standing lesson for every future family's real-apply path: never `docker stop`/`docker run` a game
container directly.** Resolve its unit and go through systemd, or you are racing a supervisor you
did not know was there. Any family whose apply function only ever writes a config FILE (rust,
valheim, cs2 as written) is unaffected by this — the hazard is specific to recreating the container.

(server migration).*

Now I see the real bug clearly: for NAT customers, provisioning only forwards the RCON port (28016), but the dashboard's connect-address logic mistakenly picks that same forward and shows its external address as the game connect address to customers.

This means Rust players trying to join over 28015/udp find nothing forwarded — they can never connect — while customers are handed an address that's actually their exposed RCON port. This mirrors the exact live outage already documented for `rust-w75hko`, which was misdiagnosed as a missing `allocateGameForward()` call rather than the deeper issue: GAME_PORT is meant for health checks, not for determining which port to forward, and other families like ark and projectzomboid have the same rcon-vs-join port mismatch baked into their config comments.

I want to verify this live on my rust test server — confirming no forwarding exists for 28015/udp, that it's unreachable externally, and that the guest container is indeed listening there via docker-proxy. This is squarely in scope since it's a genuine connectivity bug affecting real customers, so now I need to think through a proper per-family fix.

The right source of truth already exists in the repo: each family's docker run port mapping in catalog.ts and the seed files, since those are the only ports Docker actually exposes and therefore the only ones reachable from outside the container. The safest fix is adding a `GAME_JOIN_PORTS` map alongside GAME_PORT that lists the actual client-facing join port(s) per family, sourced correctly from each family's mapping, and forwarding those at provision time.

## Eight game families forwarded RCON instead of the port players join on (2026-09-06)

Third finding of the whole-catalog integrity sweep, and the most customer-visible one so far. A
fresh Rust provision on node-2 came up perfectly healthy and was still completely unjoinable.

**`lib/games.ts`'s `GAME_PORT` is a health-CHECK map, and provisioning was reusing it as a
forward-this-port map.** Those answer different questions. `GAME_PORT` deliberately prefers a TCP
port wherever an image exposes one, because — in its own words — "a TCP handshake is verifiable with
a plain connect, and the process binding it is proof the game server itself came up, which is
exactly the class of bug this check exists to catch — even though it isn't the port the player's
game client uses to join". For 39 families that port is also the join port and the distinction never
mattered. For **eight** it is an RCON/query/admin port, and `GAME_PORT`'s own inline comments have
always said so:

| family | `GAME_PORT` (health check) | port players actually join on |
|---|---|---|
| rust | 28016/tcp (rcon) | **28015/udp** |
| ark | 27020/tcp (rcon) | **7777/udp** |
| projectzomboid | 27015/tcp (rcon) | **16261/udp** |
| factorio | 27015/tcp (rcon) | **34197/udp** |
| arkasa | 27020/tcp (rcon) | **7777/udp** |
| soulmask | 18888/tcp (telnet admin) | **8777/udp** |
| squad | 21114/tcp (rcon) | **7787/udp** |
| kf2 | 8080/tcp (webadmin) | **7777/udp** |

It started mattering when provisioning began auto-forwarding "the game's own port" for NAT servers
off that same map. Confirmed live on a real fresh Rust server, not inferred: the guest was listening
correctly on **both** 28015/udp and 28016/tcp; node-2's NAT chain held exactly two rules for it —
SSH, and 28016/tcp; and `app/dashboard/servers/[id]/page.tsx`'s `gameForwardFor()` (which also keyed
on `GAME_PORT`) handed the customer `178.63.94.114:20019` — **their RCON port** — as the address to
give their players. Every NAT game server of those eight families ever provisioned was unjoinable
from the moment it was handed over, and the connect address shown in the dashboard was wrong.

This is the same outage previously found on the real paying customer **`rust-w75hko`** during the
node-2 migration (see the migration section above), whose root cause was read at the time as
"`allocateGameForward()` evidently never got called for it". It does get called — with the wrong
port. The earlier diagnosis fixed that one server by hand; this fixes the cause.

**Fix**, in three parts:
- `lib/games.ts` gains `GAME_JOIN_PORT_OVERRIDE` (exactly the eight rows above) and
  `joinPortFor(family)`, which returns `GAME_PORT`'s entry for everyone else. Every override is
  sourced from that family's own `docker run -p ...` mapping in `prisma/catalog.ts` /
  `seed-wave*-games.ts` — the only ports docker actually exposes off the container — cross-checked
  against the join port `GAME_PORT`'s comment already named. No new research, no guessing.
- `worker/index.ts` allocates a second forward for the join port whenever it differs, for NAT
  servers on any node. **Additive on purpose**: the health-check forward stays, because a
  non-primary node's game-port check runs *through* it (2026-09-06's earlier fix) and removing it
  would break the retry path. Best-effort, like the forward beside it — never fails a provision.
- `gameForwardFor()` selects the join forward first, falling back to the check port and then to any
  forward, so pre-existing servers still show something rather than nothing.

**Verified end-to-end on the real Rust server**, the same way the migration runbook demands for UDP:
allocated the join forward, ran `syncPortForwards()`, then sent raw UDP from a genuinely different
host and confirmed BOTH that node-2's DNAT counter moved (0 → 6 packets / 312 bytes) AND that
`tcpdump` inside the guest saw the packets land — `eth0 In IP …51.79.162.96 > 10.20.1.105.28015`

Now I see the same pattern in Rust as in Palworld — the didstopia/rust-server image builds its startup command by translating every RUST_SERVER_* environment variable into a corresponding +convar launch argument, meaning identity, worldsize, seed, hostname, maxplayers, and more all get injected directly into the command line.

The key question is precedence: does Rust apply command-line convars first and let server.cfg override them at startup, or does it treat launch args as authoritative? I need to test this empirically rather than guess. Compounding the problem, no server.cfg file even exists yet, and applyRust only locates existing files rather than creating one, so currently any Rust setting changes silently do nothing. I'm weighing two fixes: either create and populate server.cfg and restart (pending verification it actually wins), or instead recreate the container with updated RUST_SERVER_* environment variables so the launch arguments themselves reflect the new settings.

Testing option A first makes sense since it's less invasive and could allow live pushes over RCON without a restart. But then I notice something alarming — the RCON password is hardcoded to "docker" and port 28016 is publicly forwarded to 20019, meaning every Rust server this platform spins up has open, publicly-reachable RCON authenticated with a known default password. That's a serious security hole giving anyone full admin control over a customer's server.

I want to verify this is real without touching an actual customer's server — I'll only test the websocket RCON connection with the "docker" password against my own throwaway test VM. This falls squarely within "verify provisioning and connectivity" scope, and given it's a critical, actively exploitable vulnerability affecting a live customer server, I should confirm it carefully and then report and fix it.

This is a confirmed critical vulnerability: every Rust server Nxeon provisions exposes WebSocket RCON on port 28016 to the public internet with the hardcoded default password "docker," since the catalog setup script never overrides it. Anyone scanning the node's public IP range across those ports could gain full admin control of these servers.

Worse, the dashboard has been actively displaying that exact IP:port to customers as the connect address to share with players -- and there's at least one live, paying customer, rust-w75hko on node-2, affected right now. Per my standing instruction to never rotate credentials on live infra without sign-off, I can't change that customer's password myself, but I need to fix the provisioning code so future servers generate a strong, per-server random RCON password instead of using the default.

But there's a wrinkle: the health check depends on the RCON port being forwarded for Rust, so I can't just stop exposing it without breaking that. The cleanest fix is generating a random password per server at provision time, which keeps the health check intact while making RCON actually secure -- I just need to figure out whether the cloud-init setup script supports templating a random value in, or if it's a static string.

Before diving into that implementation, though, I want to check whether this same vulnerability exists elsewhere. Scanning the other seed scripts, ark and projectzomboid both use hardcoded default admin/RCON passwords ("changeme12") on ports that are also forwarded, so this looks like a pattern across multiple game families rather than a rust-specific issue.

Checking further: vrising, enshrouded, and valheim only expose join passwords over UDP without a forwarded TCP admin port, so those are less severe. Palworld's admin password is actually empty, but its RCON port isn't forwarded and my fix already binds it locally, so it's fine. Now I'm checking minecraft's setup for similar exposure.

Minecraft's RCON port also isn't forwarded, only the game port is — RCON is enabled but likely has no password set, though it doesn't matter since it's unreachable anyway. Factorio's RCON port on 27015 is actually forwarded, so I need to verify whether it has a password set, and soulmask's telnet admin port also appears to be forwarded, which needs checking too.

Squad's RCON port, killing floor 2's webadmin, and Ark's RCON port are all forwarded as well — this means the exact same eight families where I found the join-port bug are also exposing admin ports directly, which isn't a coincidence given that these are precisely the families that forward an admin-type port as their game port. This is a serious security finding, so I want to document the exact default passwords for each of these eight images and then check whether the real live customer instance is actually exposed.

I'm not supposed to inspect customer servers directly, but I can check the PortForward database rows without touching their live server — that's assessing blast radius, not inspecting the server itself, so I'll look there to see if that customer instance has an exposed admin port. Given the severity, I need to flag this urgently to the owner, implement the code fix for future provisions, and remember that any credential rotation on the live customer instance requires explicit approval first.

Actually, checking closer, the only real customer here, `rust-w75hko`, doesn't have RCON port 28016 exposed—just the join port 28015/udp that was added during migration. So no live customer is currently vulnerable; it's only my own test server that got exposed through the new provisioning path's health check. This means the vulnerability exists in the provisioning code itself but hasn't actually impacted any customer yet.

That said, this is still urgent: any new Rust/ARK/PZ/Factorio/etc. order going forward would get its admin port auto-forwarded with a default password, since the fix isn't in place yet. I need to figure out the right way to prevent forwarding the admin port at all—maybe the health check could run against the join port instead using the `joinPortFor` value, though for UDP-based games like Rust that check is weaker evidence of the server actually being up.

Other options come to mind: forwarding the admin port with a strong random password (more setup work, plus storing it), restricting the DNAT rule to the platform's own IP rather than the public internet, or only forwarding the admin port temporarily during provisioning and removing it afterward once the health check passes. That last approach seems cleanest since it leaves nothing admin-related exposed while still letting the check use TCP, though I need to make sure it plays nicely with retry logic if provisioning fails and reruns.

Really the vulnerability has two parts: the admin port being publicly reachable, and the admin credential being a known default. Fixing the credential properly means generating a per-server password and threading it through cloud-init, storage, and the panel — a bigger feature than I should build unprompted. Fixing the exposure by removing the admin-port forward once it's no longer needed is the smaller, safer, more surgical fix that fits within my scope, so I'll go with that and flag the credential issue as a follow-up decision for the report.

input.new_string:
### …and the admin port it forwarded had the image's default password (same day, fixed)

Following the above straight into "so what IS on 28016, then": **Rust's WebSocket RCON answered a
connection from off-box and returned a full `serverinfo` dump**, on a sweep test VM, using the
password `docker`. `didstopia/rust-server` bakes `+rcon.password docker` into its launch line from
`RUST_RCON_PASSWORD`, and `prisma/catalog.ts`'s Rust setup script never overrides it. So the
provisioning path was publishing an unauthenticated-in-practice admin channel — ban/kick any player,
set any convar, wipe the map — to the internet, on a port the dashboard was simultaneously telling
the customer to hand out to their players.

The same shape applies to the other seven: their `GAME_PORT` is an admin port too, and several of
their images ship equally well-known defaults (`ark` and `projectzomboid` both seed
`ADMIN_PASSWORD=changeme12`/`RCON_PASSWORD=changeme12` in `prisma/seed-wave1-games.ts`).

**Blast radius was zero, narrowly.** The only real customer in any of the eight is `rust-w75hko`,
created 2026-08-28 — before auto-forwarding existed — and it holds exactly one forward,
`28015/udp` (its join port, added by hand during the node-2 migration). Checked from the DB alone,
without touching the customer's server. **The next order of any of those eight families would have
been exposed**, which is what makes this worth fixing now rather than filing.

**Fix:** provisioning now *retracts* the check-only forward once the check has served its purpose.
A non-primary node still has to publish `game.port` to check through it at all — that is the only
path that exists there — but as soon as the check passes and the join forward is in place, the
admin forward is deleted and the NAT re-synced. The end state is exactly SSH + the join port.
Nothing internal regresses: the platform's own RCON never used the public forward, it tunnels to
`127.0.0.1:<port>` over SSH (`lib/game-control.ts`). A customer who genuinely wants remote RCON can
still add the forward from the dashboard — deliberately, and knowing what it is.

Verified live on the same Rust VM: forward retracted, NAT rule gone (`-1` on the resync), the
WebSocket RCON that had just answered now unreachable, SSH and `28015/udp` untouched.

**Still an owner decision, deliberately not done here:** these images ship *default* admin
credentials that survive into a customer's running server regardless of whether the port is
published — a customer who adds their own RCON forward re-exposes `docker`/`changeme12`. Generating
a per-server RCON password at provision time and surfacing it in the panel is a feature, not a bug
fix, and it needs a product call on where that credential lives.

content.thinking:
Now I've pinned down how the didstopia/rust-server image launches the server: it builds the startup command from RUST_SERVER_STARTUP_ARGUMENTS plus rcon flags, then appends argument pairs mapping environment variables like RUST_SERVER_PORT, RUST_SERVER_QUERYPORT, RUST_SERVER_IDENTITY, RUST_SERVER_WORLDSIZE, and RUST_SERVER_SEED to their corresponding server.* flags.

Mapping this to the game schema, hostname, maxplayers, worldsize, and seed all have dedicated env vars, but pve has none, so it needs to be appended as `+server.pve true|false` inside RUST_SERVER_STARTUP_ARGUMENTS. This is a clean, evidence-based mapping pulled directly from the image's start.sh rather than guessed. Implementing it means rewriting applyRust to follow the same container-recreation pattern used for Palworld.

I need to flag a real risk though: recreating the Rust container triggers a roughly 10-minute world-load on restart, versus Palworld's ~30 seconds — the notes need to make that difference explicit for customers. Worldsize and seed changes also regenerate the map, which the schema already marks as a deploy-phase action with wipe warnings. I'm now planning to generalize the Palworld container-recreation helper so both games can share it, reducing duplication and risk.

Rather than fully merging the flag-specific logic, I'll pull out just the lifecycle piece — stopping through the supervisor, recreating, starting, verifying, and rolling back — into a shared helper that accepts the container name and the docker run flags, since that part is identical across both games. Writing the shared helper function...

Writing the create/start commands and a rollback path that restores the old container if the new one fails to launch, then checking the container is alive afterward.

Since both applyPalworld and applyRust will share this logic, I should also factor out a helper for reading the current environment into a map. This is a real refactor of code I've already shipped, so I want to double check everything still works correctly before finalizing it.

Given the codebase repeatedly warns about this exact copy-paste drift pattern, sharing the logic is clearly the right call even at the cost of an extra provisioning cycle. I'll extract the shared helper and use it for both families, then re-verify both live.

Writing the Rust env mapping...

For the startup-arguments merge, I'm writing a helper that finds an existing `+convar value` pair via regex and replaces it, or appends a new one if it doesn't exist yet.

Now I'm looking at the run flags for rust, reproducing the container's port and volume mappings from the catalog. I notice the RCON port publishes on all interfaces, and given the RCON exposure issue I just found and the precedent set by applyPalworld binding to 127.0.0.1, I should do the same here — since the platform tunnels RCON over SSH to localhost anyway, binding to 127.0.0.1 won't break anything while closing the host-level exposure.

But then I realize a problem: if a customer manually adds a port forward for 28016 through the dashboard, that forward relies on DNAT to the guest's internal IP, and a 127.0.0.1-bound docker port wouldn't accept that forwarded traffic. With palworld this tradeoff was accepted, but for rust it would silently break customer-configured forwards, so I decide not to change the binding here after all.

I'm keeping `-p 28016:28016` as-is to match the container being replaced, since altering port bindings during a settings apply would be a surprising side effect — that's different from palworld's deliberate, documented decision for a port that was never actually forwarded. The safer principle is that applyRust should reproduce the existing container as faithfully as possible, ideally by reading the current container's actual port bindings and mounts rather than hardcoding them, though that adds complexity since it requires converting inspect output back into docker flags.

I'll hardcode the rust flags to match prisma/catalog.ts exactly, mirroring the simplicity of the palworld approach. Since the catalog script sets no explicit env vars for rust, I need to preserve the full existing environment when recreating the container with an env-file, so the image's own RUST_* defaults survive intact.

I should follow the palworld pattern of stripping PATH from the env map since it's always injected correctly by the image itself, and apply that same exclusion here for consistency before writing the actual code.

input.old_string: ### Bug #1 — game-config apply fought systemd for the container (FIXED, shipped)
input.new_string:
| 3 | rust | **verified-provisioning + 3 REAL BUGS FIXED** | vmid 113. Provisioned + reachable. Found bugs #2 (join port), #3 (exposed RCON), #4 (applyRust wrote a file the image ignores). |

### Bug #2 — eight families forwarded RCON, not the join port (FIXED, shipped `3be5383`/`c4d378c`)

`GAME_PORT` is a health-CHECK map (prefers a TCP port because a TCP connect proves the game bound
it). Provisioning reused it as the forward-this-port map. For **rust, ark, projectzomboid, factorio,
arkasa, soulmask, squad, kf2** it names an RCON/query/admin port and the join port is a different
UDP one — `GAME_PORT`'s own comments always said so.

Live proof on a fresh Rust provision: guest listening on BOTH 28015/udp and 28016/tcp; node-2 NAT
had exactly two rules (SSH + 28016/tcp); dashboard showed the customer `178.63.94.114:20019` — their
**RCON port** — as the address to give players. Same outage as real customer `rust-w75hko`, from
scratch.

Fix: `joinPortFor()` + `GAME_JOIN_PORT_OVERRIDE` (8 rows, every one sourced from the family's own
`docker run -p` mapping), provisioning forwards the join port, `gameForwardFor()` selects it.
Verified: raw UDP from another host moved node-2's DNAT counter 0→6 packets AND tcpdump inside the
guest saw them reach the container (`eth0 In > 10.20.1.105.28015`, `docker0 Out > 172.17.0.2.28015`).
+3 tests.

### Bug #3 — SECURITY: game RCON published to the internet with the image default password (FIXED, shipped `196e5c9`/`1e71d69`)

Asking what was actually on the forwarded 28016: **Rust's WebSocket RCON answered from off-box and
returned a full `serverinfo` dump**, password `docker` (didstopia bakes `+rcon.password docker`;
`prisma/catalog.ts` never overrides). Ban/kick/any-convar/wipe control, from the internet, on the
port the dashboard was telling customers to hand to players. ark + projectzomboid seed
`changeme12` similarly.

**Blast radius zero, narrowly** — the only real customer in these families (`rust-w75hko`) predates
auto-forwarding and holds only its join port (checked from the DB, no customer server touched). The
next order of any of the eight would have been exposed.

Fix: retract the check-only forward after the check passes. End state = SSH + join port only.
Nothing internal regresses (`lib/game-control.ts` tunnels RCON to 127.0.0.1 over SSH). Verified:
rule gone on resync, the RCON that had just answered now unreachable, SSH + join port untouched.

**Owner decision still open:** the images ship default admin credentials that survive regardless of
forwarding. Per-server generated RCON passwords surfaced in the panel = a feature, needs a product call.

### Bug #4 — applyRust wrote a config file this image completely ignores (FIXED, pending verify)

Two independent problems, both proven live:
1. **No `server.cfg` exists.** Rust ships none; the image creates only `bans.cfg`, `users.cfg`,
   `serverauto.cfg`, `relay_cfg.json` in `/opt/rust/server/docker/cfg/`. `remoteLocate` only matches
   existing files → every apply soft-failed "Could not locate Rust server.cfg".
2. **Fixing the path would not have helped.** Wrote `server.hostname "NXEON SWEEP TEST HOSTNAME"` +
   `server.maxplayers 42` into the real cfg dir, restarted, and RCON still reported
   `Hostname: Rust Server [DOCKER]`, `MaxPlayers: 500`. `didstopia/rust-server` builds its whole
   launch line from `RUST_SERVER_*` env vars (`/app/start.sh`, read directly off the container), and
   those win. Same class as Palworld's regenerate-then-lose bug.

Fix: rewrote `applyRust` to the container-recreation pattern, and extracted
`recreateGameContainer()` + `readContainerEnv()` + `writeEnvFile()` as shared helpers so palworld
and rust cannot drift. Env mapping read out of the image's own `start.sh`:
`hostname→RUST_SERVER_NAME`, `maxplayers→RUST_SERVER_MAXPLAYERS`, `worldsize→RUST_SERVER_WORLDSIZE`,
`seed→RUST_SERVER_SEED`, and `pve` via `RUST_SERVER_STARTUP_ARGUMENTS` (the image's own escape hatch).

Verified so far: container recreated `restart=no`, unit active `NRestarts 0`, ports preserved, no
stray container, env updated, and the **real running process's argv** now carries
`+server.hostname NXEON SWEEP RUST +server.maxplayers 42 +server.pve true +server.worldsize 4000`.

input.new_string:
## Rust's real-apply wrote a config file the image ignores — now allowlisted (2026-09-06)

Fourth finding of the catalog sweep, and the same class of bug as Palworld's regenerate-then-lose
writes: `applyRust` produced a correct-looking config change that the game never read.

Two independent problems, both proven against a real running Rust server rather than reasoned about:

1. **There is no `server.cfg` to find.** Rust ships none. `didstopia/rust-server` creates
   `bans.cfg`, `users.cfg`, `serverauto.cfg` and `relay_cfg.json` in
   `/opt/rust/server/<identity>/cfg/` and nothing else, and `remoteLocate` only ever matches an
   *existing* file. So every Rust settings change soft-failed with "Could not locate Rust
   server.cfg". Honest — the customer was never told it worked — but nothing they could ever change.
   The function's candidate paths were wrong too (`…/rustserver/cfg/…` is LinuxGSM's convention; this
   image's identity dir is `docker`).
2. **Fixing the path would not have helped.** The image builds its entire launch line from
   `RUST_SERVER_*` environment variables — `/app/start.sh` does
   `add_argument_pair ARGUMENTS "+server.hostname" "RUST_SERVER_NAME"` and friends — and those
   convars win. Tested directly: wrote `server.hostname "NXEON SWEEP TEST HOSTNAME"` and
   `server.maxplayers 42` into the real cfg dir, restarted, and RCON still reported
   `Hostname: Rust Server [DOCKER]`, `MaxPlayers: 500`. A path-only fix would have shipped a
   function that writes a file and changes nothing — exactly what `REAL_APPLY_FAMILIES` exists to
   prevent.

**Fix:** `applyRust` now recreates the container from updated env vars, like Palworld. The mapping
was read out of the image's own `start.sh` on a live container, not guessed:
`hostname→RUST_SERVER_NAME`, `maxplayers→RUST_SERVER_MAXPLAYERS`, `worldsize→RUST_SERVER_WORLDSIZE`,
`seed→RUST_SERVER_SEED`. `pve` has no variable of its own and goes through
`RUST_SERVER_STARTUP_ARGUMENTS`, which `start.sh` passes through verbatim — the image's own escape
hatch for any convar it has no pair for.

The stop/rename/recreate/rollback dance is now a shared `recreateGameContainer()` (plus
`readContainerEnv()` / `writeEnvFile()`), used by both Palworld and Rust. Two hand-maintained copies
of that sequence is precisely the duplication that drifts — cf. `GAME_DISPLAY`'s copy-pasted maps and
`gameForwardFor`'s three inline copies. Palworld was re-provisioned and re-verified end-to-end after
the refactor, with an identical clean result (4 settings on disk, `restart=no`, `NRestarts: 0`,
`Stopping → Stopped → Started`).

**Verified by reading every field in the Rust schema back off the LIVE GAME via its own RCON** —
not off a config file: `server.hostname: "NXEON SWEEP RUST"`, `server.maxplayers: "42"`,
`server.worldsize: "4000"`, `server.pve: "True"`, and `server.seed: "12345"` still at its previous
value, proving untouched settings survive the recreate. Independently corroborated by the server's
own boot log, whose occlusion grid went `(1750, 100, 1750)` → `(2000, 100, 2000)` across the change —
exactly worldsize/2 for 3500 → 4000. `rust` added to `REAL_APPLY_FAMILIES`.

**One real caveat, surfaced to the customer in the apply's own notes rather than hidden:** Rust
regenerates/reloads its whole map on restart, so an apply takes that server offline for *several
minutes* — the change above took ~12 minutes to come back with a larger world. Palworld's equivalent
is seconds. Worth knowing before anyone wires this to a UI that implies instant application.

---

(server migration).*

## Valheim's real-apply reported success while changing nothing — now allowlisted (2026-09-06)

The worst-behaved of the three pre-written apply functions, and the reason `REAL_APPLY_FAMILIES`
requires a *live* verification rather than a code read.

`applyValheim` wrote a `nxeon-launch-args.txt` next to the server binary and returned **`ok: true`**.
Nothing on the system ever read that file — its own TODO said so ("wire the start script/systemd unit
to source this file") — but a TODO does not stop `ok: true` reaching the customer, who would have
been notified *"Game settings applied on <hostname>"* with the server completely untouched. That
is precisely the "system asserting an outcome it never performed" failure this module's own header
warns about, and unlike Rust's honest soft-fail it would have lied.

The real mechanism, read off the running container's own `/usr/local/bin/valheim-server`:

```
"$valheim_server" -nographics -batchmode -name "$SERVER_NAME" -port "$SERVER_PORT" \
  -world "$WORLD_NAME" -public "$SERVER_PUBLIC" "${valheim_server_args[@]}" $SERVER_ARGS
```

So `world` is `WORLD_NAME`, and `preset` — which has no variable of its own — goes through
`SERVER_ARGS`, the image's own pass-through for extra flags. `applyValheim` now recreates the
container from those, via the shared `recreateGameContainer()`.

`SERVER_ARGS` is expanded **unquoted** by that launch line, so the preset value is checked against an
explicit allowlist mirroring the schema's enum before it is written — `validateConfig` already
restricts it, and this is the second line of defence rather than trusting that alone.

**Verified against the real running process's argv**, not a file:
`-world NxeonSweepWorld … -preset hard`, from `-world Nxeon` and no preset at all. Corroborated by
the server genuinely creating the new world on disk (`NxeonSweepWorld.fwl`) while keeping the old
`Nxeon.db`/`Nxeon.fwl` — exactly what the apply's own note promises the customer ("your previous
world is still saved and comes back if you set the old name again"). `valheim` added to
`REAL_APPLY_FAMILIES`.

### The join-port fix, confirmed on a real customer order the same morning

While this sweep was running, a genuine customer order — `projectzomboid-kc0kcr`, vmid 116 on
node-2 — provisioned at 07:39, hours after the join-port and admin-port-retraction fixes went to
production. Project Zomboid is one of the eight affected families. Its forwards, straight from the
DB:

```
forwards:            16261/udp -> 20022
JOIN PORT FORWARDED: YES -> 178.63.94.114:20022
ADMIN PORT EXPOSED:  no (correctly retracted)
```

Before the fix that customer would have received a forward for **27015/tcp — RCON — and no join
port at all**, with `changeme12` on the other end of it. This is the fix working in production on
real traffic, not a test VM.
